svg.title: Fine-tuning changes form, not facts
svg.desc: Two contrasting boxes. Form and behavior, such as output format, tone, and narrow task compliance, sits on the left as something fine-tuning can reliably learn. Facts and knowledge, such as a changed policy or a new product name, sits on the right as something fine-tuning cannot reliably learn. A caption below illustrates this with the Romeo-to-Bob substitution experiment, where a fine-tuning run failed to teach a model a new fact.
svg.text: output format · tone · a narrow task done the same way every time
a policy that changed · a new product name · an updated table
The Romeo-to-Bob experiment: every "Romeo" in Shakespeare's text was replaced with "Bob," and a model was
fine-tuned on that modified text to see whether it would learn the substitution as a new fact.
Prompted afterward with "Romeo," the model's completion never produced "Bob." Next-token prediction loss on
a small training set does not rewrite what the model already knows, only how it expresses what it knows.
